title: My mental model of effective instruction
author: Benjamin Riley
summary: Responding to what he calls the Great Instructional Debates of 2026, Benjamin Riley lays out his own four-step mental model of effective instruction, grounded in cognitive science and his experience training novice teachers. The steps are to have a clear learning goal, to generate effortful thinking about it, to plan for failure, and to make learning visible through assessment. He supports structured routines for novices but warns that routines and scaffolds are not enough and can deceive teachers into valuing orderly classrooms over thinking. He argues that scripted lessons run aground because no script can anticipate a school day, and that teachers must think about the why of each lesson, which is why he is hostile to AI lesson planning. On assessment he rejects relying on vibes and calls out higher education for rarely checking learning along the way. His summary is that routines are mostly good, scripts are always bad, and teachers should avoid AI for planning.
points: Start with a learning goal, not with fun, since engagement should serve what the teacher wants students to learn.
To learn something, students must think about it, so lessons are judged by whether they generate the right thinking, not by surface routines.
Teachers should plan for what happens when an activity fails, and unscripted professional judgement matters because school days are unpredictable.
Riley objects to AI lesson planning because the why of a lesson is where professional expertise lives and should not be automated.
Formative assessment must supply observable evidence of learning, a practice he says higher education often neglects.
quotes: The learning goal is what you want students to learn. Seems obvious, right? Yet you might be surprised how often this critical first step is not deeply considered by novice educators, who are often seduced by non-learning goals, such as, “will my students find this fun?
There is at least one universal cognitive truth about building knowledge — to learn something new, you have to think about that something.
Routines and scaffolds are not sufficient to ensure effortful thinking by students, and they may even be deceptive if teachers start to think that orderly classrooms are the primary end-goal.
Teachers must imagine how things might go wrong within a lesson, and have a plan for what to do next.
Life is inherently unpredictable, and so too are lessons — teaching is improv theater, not a paint-by-numbers exercise.
Relying on a mindless tool to generate text that purportedly constitutes a “lesson plan” is generally not helpful toward that end, and I wish people in education would stop pretending otherwise.
In sum, routines mostly good (especially for novice teachers), scripts always bad, avoid AI please, and remember to always think about the “why?” of the lesson.
